lessons.title: Mixed practice without a calculator
lessons.summary: Practise the written methods and quick checks used in the non-calculator part of Checkpoint.
lessons.objective: Practise the written methods and quick checks used in the non-calculator part of Checkpoint.
lessons.before: For a mixed revision session, choose a method before carrying out each calculation.
lessons.ideas:
Use equivalent fractions, cancellation and exact integer steps. Leave a line that a reader can follow.

Use the right angle to identify the hypotenuse. Keep any exact fractions until a value must be rounded.

For each answer, say what count, centre or spread you have calculated. Use exact values when a fraction is simpler.
lessons.method:
Show the step that explains your answer.

Show the step that explains your answer.

Show the step that explains your answer.
mistakes: An answer typed into a short check can still benefit from written working.
Do not apply the Pythagoras rule before checking the right angle.
The sum of a set gives only the first step of the mean.

examples.title: Non-calculator: a craft sale
examples.question:
A sale starts with 20 packs in a ratio of 6 red to 4 blue. One half of all packs are sold before lunch. After lunch the organisers sell the equivalent of \(2\) two-pack boxes. One half-box means one pack.

  1. Find the number of packs sold before lunch.

    [2]

  2. Find how many packs were left after both sales.

    [2]

  3. Find how many red packs there were before the first sale.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) The total was even. Divide it by 2.

\(10\)

(b) The afternoon sale represents 4 packs. Subtract those from the packs remaining at lunch.

\(6\)

(c) There were twice as many packs as one complete set of ratio parts.

\(12\)

examples.title: Non-calculator: a right-angled court
examples.question:
A right-angled triangular court has legs 64 m and 120 m.

  1. Find the diagonal edge length, in metres.

    [2]

  2. The long edge is marked in three equal lengths. Write the length of each part.

    [1]

  3. Find the triangular court area.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Square the legs and add to get 18496. Take the square root.

\(136\)

(b) Divide the edge length by 3.

\(\frac{136}{3}\) m.

(c) The two legs are perpendicular, so one can be base and the other height.

\(3840\) square metres.

examples.title: Non-calculator: compare game results
examples.question:
A class records wins on three days. There are 10, 7 and 2 wins respectively.

  1. Find the mean number of wins per day.

    [2]

  2. Find the median and range.

    [2]

  3. Would three days alone establish a long-term change?

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) The total is 19. Divide it by three days.

\(\frac{19}{3}\)

(b) Sort the three values. Use the centre value for the median and the extremes for the range.

Median 7. Range 8.

(c) A short set may be affected by ordinary variation.

No. More observations can show whether the pattern continues.

lessons.title: Mixed practice with a calculator
lessons.summary: Use a calculator accurately and explain why a method and rounding decision fit each question.
lessons.objective: Use a calculator accurately and explain why a method and rounding decision fit each question.
lessons.before: Save the full result of one step before using it in the next.
lessons.ideas:
For repeated percentage changes, multiply each current value by its proper factor. Round at the end.

A circle's area uses the radius squared. Keep a full π value when a practical calculation follows.

Grams per cubic centimetre means grams divided by cubic centimetres. Multiply density by volume to recover mass.

examples.title: Calculator: changing sign-up numbers
examples.question:
A club starts with 370 sign-ups. Its total grows by 8% in each of two years.

  1. Find the predicted final total to the nearest whole person.

    [2]

  2. Explain how rounding during the calculation can affect the answer.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) Multiply the initial total by 1.08 twice. The unrounded result is 431.568.

\(432\)

(b) Keep the exact or calculator value until the final result.

A rounding change in year one is multiplied during year two.

examples.title: Calculator: measure a circular area
examples.question:
A circular flower bed has diameter 17 m.

  1. Find its area in square metres, rounded to 2 decimal places.

    [2]

  2. Find how many 3-square-metre packs are needed to cover the bed.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Halve the diameter to get a radius of 8.5 m.

Multiply the square of this radius by π.

\(226.98\)

(b) Divide the exact area by 3, then round up because part of a pack still uses a whole pack.

76 packs.

examples.title: Calculator: compare mass per unit volume
examples.question:
A solid block has volume 108 cubic centimetres and mass 64.8 grams.

  1. Calculate its density in grams per cubic centimetre.

    [2]

  2. A same-material block has volume 216 cubic centimetres. Calculate its mass.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Use mass divided by volume.

\(\frac{3}{5}\)

(b) With density fixed, doubling the volume doubles the mass.

129.6 grams.
